items.title: How old is Seoul's Tram 381?
items.summary: Hwang Haejin dates Seoul's preserved Tram 381 to 1944–45 by comparing vehicle types, drawings and company records.
items.caption:
How old is Seoul's Tram 381?

Hwang Haejin revisits a familiar museum object: Tram 381, preserved at the Seoul Museum of History. The study challenges its conventional dating to the 1930s, arguing instead that it was made in 1944–45 at a Nippon Sharyo factory in Incheon.

How can a historian establish an object's age when its history is uncertain? Hwang compares vehicle types, technical drawings, company records and contemporary newspapers. The tram's semi-steel construction provides an initial clue: this type entered Gyeongseong, colonial Seoul, no earlier than 1929.

The numbering system then narrows the possibilities. Company records identify No. 335 as the latest comparable vehicle in 1939. Hwang establishes that numbers were assigned within vehicle categories in acquisition order, making No. 381 later than that benchmark. Records from the 1940s support the final 1944–45 estimate.

The argument turns a question about one tram into a lesson in historical method: a number becomes evidence only when we understand the system that produced it. Looking closely at an everyday object can unsettle an apparently settled chronology.

황해진 (2020), 「서울역사박물관 소장 전차 ‘381호’ 제작 연대 및 제작지 검토」 [Dating and Locating the Manufacture of Tram 381], 서울과 역사 106, 149–178.
https://doi.org/10.22827/seoul.2020..106.004
https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/landing/article.kci?arti_id=ART002641055

items.title: Why preserve another family's records?
items.summary: Lee Jung-ran links late Goryeo genealogical records to bilateral kinship and equal inheritance.
items.caption:
Why did a late Goryeo household preserve another family’s register?

Lee Jung-ran investigates how equal inheritance and bilateral kinship shaped genealogical records in late Goryeo. Rather than treating household registers and lineage charts as neutral family trees, the study asks what material interests made these records worth keeping.

Drawing on household registers, lineage charts and pedigrees later copied into genealogies or preserved by particular families, Lee finds that the records could reach well beyond a narrow paternal line. They included the ancestors of sons-in-law, and being listed did not necessarily mean that everyone lived in one household. More strikingly, the family named in a record was sometimes different from the family that preserved it: documents concerning the Nam, Im, Lee or Han families survived in the collections of various Yu and Hong lineages.

Lee argues that this pattern reflected more than pride in ancestry. Equal inheritance both emerged from and helped sustain a bilateral understanding of kinship. Because descendants connected through women could possess claims to family property, preserving records across surname lines offered evidence that might matter in a future inheritance dispute.

The study shows how archival survival can reveal social structure. A genealogy was also a practical document whose value depended on property, legal claims and ties through both women and men.

이정란 (2015), 「고려시대 계보기록과 재산 상속 - 여계(女系) 가문의 상속권을 중심으로 -」, 여성과 역사 23, 1–36.
English title: “Genealogical Records during the Period of Goryeo Dynasty and Women’s Right of Inheritance.”
https://doi.org/10.22511/women..23.201512.1
https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/landing/article.kci?arti_id=ART002069766

items.title: How did Jeon Tae-il’s story become a call for change?
items.summary: Cho Young-rae’s nonfiction biography follows Jeon Tae-il’s garment work, labor organizing, and call to enforce Korea’s Labor Standards Act. First published in Korean in 1983, the book carried Jeon’s story to later generations and was used in labor education.
items.caption:
Monthly Classics: Jeon Tae-il’s story, told by Cho Young-rae

어느 청년 노동자의 삶과 죽음 — *The Life and Death of a Young Worker* (descriptive English translation). By Cho Young-rae (조영래); first Korean edition, 1983.

Cho’s nonfiction biography follows Jeon Tae-il (1948–1970), a garment worker at Seoul’s Pyeonghwa Market who documented the conditions faced by workers in the clothing workshops. Drawing on Jeon’s diaries and notes, as well as testimony from his mother and acquaintances, Cho traces Jeon’s work, efforts to organize fellow workers, and demand that the Labor Standards Act be enforced. The book brings personal testimony into labor history, showing how questions of legal protection and human dignity were experienced in everyday working life.

The manuscript was completed in 1976 and first appeared in Japanese in 1978; the Korean edition followed in 1983 under the title *A Young Worker’s Life and Death*. Cho’s name was made public with a revised edition in 1991. Seoul National University’s archive records that the book carried Jeon’s story from 1970s student circles to later generations and that the manuscript was used for education at labor sites. That documented readership and educational use help explain the book’s lasting place in Korean nonfiction and labor history. We feature it as a classic because of this documented intergenerational reach and educational influence.

Sources: Tae-il Memorial Museum — https://taeil.org/permanent7 · Seoul National University Archives — https://archives.snu.ac.kr/DAS/H/H3/3/H3_3_02_P01.do?colidx=362&colnumber=COL-2017-0018 · Tae-il Foundation chronology — https://chuntaeil.org/content/about_03

items.title: Professor Lee Yaechan Publishes Research on Asian Bond Markets and China–ASEAN Financial Connectivity
items.summary: Chen Li, Yaechan Lee and Huanhuan Zheng trace how official cooperation helped deepen regional bond-market integration.
items.caption:
Professor Lee Yaechan has published “From financial regionalism to capital market regionalization: Asian bond market development and China-ASEAN financial connectivity” in The Pacific Review, coauthored with Chen Li and Huanhuan Zheng.

The article asks whether the official financial cooperation developed in East Asia since the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis has produced closer connections between the region’s capital markets. It distinguishes financial regionalism, organized through cooperation between governments, from capital market regionalization, understood as the integration of markets through cross-border investment. The distinction makes it possible to examine whether institution building has translated into changes in investment patterns.

The authors use the IMF’s Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey for 1997–2024 to investigate regional investment in debt securities. They identify a significant increase in intraregional portfolio investment, driven largely by China’s emergence as a major regional creditor after 2008. They then use process tracing of the Asian Bond Markets Initiative to examine how official cooperation contributed to this development.

State-led cooperation helped deepen regional bond-market integration.

The authors argue that regional institution building and China’s strategic opening to portfolio investment substantially strengthened China–ASEAN bond-market connectivity. Their account connects changes in investment patterns to the cooperative frameworks through which governments sought to develop regional markets. The study’s significance lies in showing how market integration can be rooted in official cooperation: regional institutions matter not only as agreements between states, but also through their relationship with cross-border capital-market activity.

Chen Li, Yaechan Lee and Huanhuan Zheng (2026), “From financial regionalism to capital market regionalization: Asian bond market development and China-ASEAN financial connectivity,” The Pacific Review, published online 21 October 2026. https://doi.org/10.1080/09512748.2026.2749551
